01-logic-computability: Proofs can be checked mechanically. Once axioms and rules of inference are explicit, a proof is a finite object a procedure can inspect. Checking shows that a conclusion follows from the axioms, not that the axioms say what we intended.

Checking, searching and deciding are different tasks. Searching through candidate proofs finds one if it exists, but may run forever when none does. A decision procedure must always stop with a correct yes or no.

A computation is a run of configurations. A configuration is exactly the information needed to resume. A Turing machine fixes the elementary steps, and because its rule table is finite data, one universal machine can simulate every other.

The Church–Turing thesis concerns what can be computed, not how fast. It links the informal idea of an effective method to Turing machines. Quantum computers in the standard model compute no new functions; they can change the resources a task needs.

No algorithm decides halting in general. Feeding a supposed halting decider a program built to do the opposite of its prediction yields a contradiction. Particular programs can still be analysed, and an analyser may sometimes answer “unknown.”

Undecidability and incompleteness are different limits. One says no always-correct terminating procedure exists; the other says a consistent, effectively axiomatized theory with enough arithmetic leaves some statement neither provable nor refutable.

Determinism is not reversibility. A deterministic step fixes the next configuration; only a one-to-one step lets us recover the previous one. Quantum evolution between measurements must be reversible, so useful computations have to preserve information.
02-boolean-reversible-computation: Tasks become Boolean functions. An encoding turns every task into a function on bit strings. A truth table specifies the function completely, but it has \(2^n\) rows and says nothing about how to compute it.

Every Boolean function is a polynomial modulo two. With XOR as addition and AND as multiplication, \(f\) is the sum of detectors for the rows where it equals one. So every function has a circuit, though not necessarily a small one.
NAND is universal. NOT, AND and XOR can all be built from NAND gates alone. Classical circuits may also copy a bit to several gates (fan-out) at no cost.

Erasure has a minimum physical cost. In the standard isothermal setting, erasing an unknown bit releases at least \(k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\) of heat (Landauer’s principle). Logical reversibility removes this forced cost but not other dissipation, and running an irreversible gate slowly does not make it reversible.

Keeping the input makes any function reversible. The map \(U_f:(x,t)\mapsto(x,\,t\oplus f(x))\) is its own inverse even when \(f\) merges inputs; the retained input is what makes the larger map one-to-one.

Controlled gates compute reversibly. A control bit survives the gate and selects a reversible update of the target. CNOT computes XOR, Toffoli computes AND, and with clean workspace Toffoli (or Fredkin) gates implement any Boolean circuit.

Workspace is uncomputed, not erased. Copy the answer into a fresh register, then run the computation backward so that only the input and the answer remain. In quantum computation, leftover records of the computation would also destroy interference.
03-amplitudes-interference: States and transitions share one description. A state assigns a weight to each configuration, written \(\sum_iv_i\ket i\), and a step \(S\) assigns a weight \(\bra jS\ket i\) to each arrow from \(i\) to \(j\). Deterministic, nondeterministic and probabilistic rules differ in how many arrows leave a configuration and in what the weights mean.

Endpoints are computed by products and sums. Multiply weights along a path (product rule) and add the paths that end at the same configuration (sum rule). For a whole state, \(v'_j=\sum_i\bra jS\ket i\,v_i\), or in kets \(S\ket i=\sum_j\bra jS\ket i\,\ket j\).

Signed weights allow cancellation. With nonnegative weights, adding a path can never lower a total; with signed weights, nonzero contributions can cancel. The Hadamard step uses this to spread a definite input and then undo itself: \(H^2=I\).

Complex amplitudes go further. Complex weights permit steps such as a square root of NOT, which no real rule allows. A configuration with amplitude \(v_j\) has probability \(|v_j|^2\). This is a postulate that the examples motivate, not a derivation.

Preserving probability constrains every step. For every input state, total probability stays one only if each configuration’s outgoing amplitudes are normalized and the cross sums between different inputs vanish.

Add amplitudes first, then square. Paths to a common endpoint interfere, constructively or destructively. A global phase changes no probability, while a relative phase changes the probabilities produced by later steps.

Path records destroy interference. A record of which path was taken sends the paths to different complete configurations, so they cannot cancel, whether or not anyone reads the record. Uncomputing the record restores the interference.
04-states-measurement: States are vectors. The weighted sum \(\ket\psi=\sum_iv_i\ket i\) becomes a column of amplitudes, and its bookkeeping rules become vector addition and multiplication by a number. The kets \(\ket0,\ket1\) form the computational basis.

Inner products are transition amplitudes. The amplitude for finding a normalized state \(\ket\phi\), given \(\ket\psi\), is \(\braket\phi\psi=\sum_j\phi_j^*\psi_j\), and its squared magnitude is the probability. Normalization reads \(\braket\psi\psi=1\), and orthogonal states have zero overlap.

Operations are matrices. The entry \(U_{ji}=\bra jU\ket i\) is the arrow weight from \(i\) to \(j\), so matrix–vector multiplication performs the path sums, and the matrix product \(VU\) is the two-step sum rule, with the rightmost matrix acting first.

Probability-preserving operations are unitary. Outgoing normalization and the cross-sum condition say that the columns are orthonormal, \(U^\dagger U=I\). The adjoint, which reverses each arrow and conjugates its amplitude, is then the inverse; for a general matrix it is not.

The postulates. A pure state is a unit vector, up to global phase, and closed systems evolve unitarily. An ideal measurement in an orthonormal basis gives outcome \(j\) with probability \(|\braket{b_j}\psi|^2\) and leaves the state \(\ket{b_j}\). These are physical assumptions, not consequences of the path arithmetic.

Measurement is not unitary. It keeps one projected component, which is why a measurement between two Hadamard steps spoils their return to \(\ket0\). Changing the measurement basis changes the question asked, not the prepared state.

Composite systems use the tensor product. Dimensions multiply, and independent preparations give product states. A joint state such as \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), whose amplitudes do not factor, is entangled.
05-quantum-model: The quantum model. Encode the input as a state, apply a prescribed unitary \(U_f\), and measure. The output state fixes the probabilities, but one run returns one classical result, not the list of amplitudes.

Programs compose gates. The overall unitary is the product \(U_T\cdots U_1\), with the first gate rightmost. Naming the product \(U_f\) does not remove its cost: qubits, gates, depth, repetitions, initialization and readout all count.
Interference does the computing. \(HZH=X\): the \(Z\) changes a relative sign that the final \(H\) converts into a certain outcome. Omit \(Z\), or measure in between, and the effect disappears.

Relative phase becomes measurable. With a phase gate \(R_\phi\) between two Hadamards, \(p(0)=(1+\cos\phi)/2\). The phase is invisible in the probabilities just before the final gate, which turns it into a difference in outcomes.

The Pauli matrices form a complete basis. \(I\), \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) each square to the identity, and every single-qubit operator is a unique linear combination of them, for example \(H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2\).

Completeness is not universality. A linear combination of matrices is not a sequence of gates. Pauli gates applied in sequence only ever reach basis states (up to phase), so continuous rotations such as \(R_x(\theta)\) are an extra capability.
One qubit shows the model, not an advantage. A speedup claim needs a family of growing tasks and a comparison of costs under stated access rules.
06-composite-systems: Registers are tensor products. An \(n\)-qubit register has \(2^n\) basis strings, and independent preparations combine by the tensor product. A local gate acts as \(U\otimes I\), while a controlled gate such as CNOT acts on two qubits jointly.

Entanglement is failure to factor. A superposition of joint configurations may still be a product state. A pure state is entangled when no pair of local vectors reproduces its amplitudes; \(H\) followed by CNOT turns \(\ket{00}\) into \(\ket{\Phi^+}=(\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\).

Joint amplitudes give every probability. Joint, marginal and conditional probabilities all come from squared joint amplitudes. Measuring part of a register keeps the terms that match the outcome and renormalizes them.

Correlation alone does not prove entanglement. A classical mixture of \(00\) and \(11\) gives the same counts in the computational basis. Measuring after \(H\otimes H\) separates the coherent Bell state from the mixture.

No-cloning. No unitary copies every unknown state, because unitaries preserve inner products and two states that can both be copied must be equal or orthogonal. Known states, or states promised to be orthogonal, can still be copied.

No-signalling and teleportation. Operations on one half of an entangled pair do not change the statistics of the other half. Teleportation moves an unknown state using a shared Bell pair and two classical bits. It works for all four outcomes, and it creates no copy and no faster-than-light signal.

Parallel evaluation is not parallel readout. Applying \(U_f\) to a uniform superposition gives \(\sum_x\ket x\ket{f(x)}\), but a measurement returns one random input–value pair. Parallelism helps only when later interference turns many values into one useful bit, and that requires a target that keeps no record of the branch.
07-queries-phase-kickback: Queries make comparisons fair. When a function is available only through a black box, we count its uses. Deciding whether a one-bit function is constant or balanced needs two classical queries, because one value leaves both possibilities open.
Quantum queries are reversible. The oracle is the reversible embedding \(U_f\ket{x,y}=\ket{x,\,y\oplus f(x)}\), and one use of it, on any state, is one query.

Holding both values is not knowing both. Querying a superposition places both function values in the state, but measuring returns one random pair. A blank target also records the input branch, which blocks the interference needed for readout.

Phase kickback. With the target in \(\ket-\), \(U_f\ket x\ket-=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\). The target keeps no record, and the function value becomes a sign on the input amplitude. If \(f\) is computed by a circuit, compute–phase–uncompute does the same, at the cost of running the circuit and its inverse.

Deutsch’s algorithm. Prepare \(\ket+\ket-\), query once, apply \(H\) to the input and measure: \(0\) means constant and \(1\) means balanced, with certainty. The outcome depends only on whether the two signs agree, never on the individual values.

What the separation means. One query against two is a statement about a stated access model with coherent oracle use, not about hardware speed. It needs all four stages: coherent preparation, phase encoding, recombination and readout.
08-circuits-universality: Reading circuits. Diagrams run left to right while matrix products act right to left. Gates on disjoint wires commute and can run in parallel, and a labelled box such as \(U_f\) hides gates whose cost the diagram does not show.
Two kinds of control. Classical control uses a measured bit to choose a later gate; coherent control acts on an unmeasured qubit and preserves superposition. Teleportation needs both.

Building blocks. Rotation gates \(R_P(\theta)=\cos\tfrac\theta2\,I-i\sin\tfrac\theta2\,P\) give turns of any size, and controlled-\(U=\ket0\bra0\otimes I+\ket1\bra1\otimes U\). Hadamards on the target turn CNOT into controlled-\(Z\).

Oracles and reflections are circuits too. A phase oracle marks a string with \(X\) gates around a multi-controlled phase flip, or by compute–phase–uncompute. The reflection about the uniform state is \(D=H^{\otimes n}(2\ket{0^n}\bra{0^n}-I)H^{\otimes n}\).

Universality needs entanglement. One-qubit gates alone map product states to product states. CNOT together with arbitrary one-qubit unitaries builds every finite-register unitary. That settles possibility, not cost: a generic unitary needs an exponentially long circuit.

Finite gate sets approximate. A finite set such as Clifford+T cannot synthesize every unitary exactly, but it can approximate one to any tolerance. The errors of approximated gates add at most linearly, \(\sum_i\epsilon_i\).

Real cost is more than a query count. It also includes gate count, depth, width (ancillas), uniform circuit families, connectivity (extra SWAPs), data loading and readout, and noise. Error correction protects logical information without cloning it.
09-amplitude-amplification: Search starts by marking with phase. Classical unstructured search for one marked label among \(N\) needs order \(N\) queries. A quantum search starts from the uniform state \(\ket s\) and marks by phase, \(O_f\ket x=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\); the mark alone changes no probability.
Reflection about the mean amplifies. \(D=2\ket s\bra s-I\) sends each amplitude \(a_x\) to \(2\mu-a_x\). For four items, one marking and one reflection find the marked label with certainty.

The search lives in a plane. Grouping marked and unmarked labels into \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\) keeps the whole evolution in two dimensions, where \(\ket s\) makes an angle \(\theta\) with the unmarked direction, \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{M/N}\).

Two reflections make a rotation. Each Grover iteration \(DO_f\) rotates the state by \(2\theta\), so after \(k\) iterations the success probability is \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\). It peaks near \(k\approx\pi/(4\theta)\), which is order \(\sqrt{N/M}\) iterations.

Stopping is part of the algorithm. Iterating past the peak lowers the success probability. When \(M\) is unknown, randomized iteration counts with a verifying query keep the order \(\sqrt{N/M}\) cost, but cannot prove that nothing is marked.

Amplitude amplification generalizes search. Any preparation \(A\) with success probability \(p\) is amplified by the reflections \(A(2\ket0\bra0-I)A^\dagger\) and \(I-2P_G\) in order \(1/\sqrt p\) rounds instead of \(1/p\). This requires coherent access to \(A\), its inverse and the success test, and each round costs about \(2C_A+C_G\).
10-complexity-advantage: Compare like with like. A speed claim needs the same task, input encoding, size measure, access model and success criterion on both sides. An integer \(N\) has about \(\log_2N\) input bits, so \(N\) steps is exponential in the input length.
Asymptotic notation. \(O\), \(\Omega\) and \(\Theta\) describe growth up to constant factors. They hide constants and crossover sizes, and they do not specify the model of computation.
Resources differ. Query, gate and space complexity count different things. A query advantage may or may not survive once each query and the input preparation are implemented.

Complexity classes. P, NP, BPP and BQP classify decision problems by the resources needed to solve them. \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\), but whether BQP is larger, or contains NP, is unknown. Fast quantum factoring is an advantage over known classical methods, not a proven separation.

Upper versus lower bounds. An upper bound exhibits one algorithm; a lower bound covers every algorithm in the model. Unstructured search needs \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) queries, so Grover’s algorithm is optimal at \(\Theta(\sqrt N)\). The polynomial method gives a second proof: after \(T\) queries, acceptance probabilities are polynomials of degree at most \(2T\).

The scope of quantum advantage. Quantum computers compute no uncomputable functions, and they face their own limits: no-cloning, sampled readout, and the costs of preparation, oracles and noise. A convincing claim states the task, the access model, an observable answer with a success guarantee, and the full cost.
